sources.title: Ichiyō Higuchi (Q237948), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-01): English label 'Ichiyō Higuchi', description 'Japanese writer', born 1872-05-02, died 1896-11-23, Korean label 히구치 이치요. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Higuchi Ichiyō' (full article read, about 300 words; page revised 28 April 2026). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: poet and novelist, the most important Japanese woman writer of her period, whose characteristic works dealt with the licensed pleasure quarters of Tokyo; study of classical literature at a poetry school, the encouragement of a classmate's published fiction, her literary diary of 1891 to 1896 (Wakabakage), her decision to ignore her mentor's advice to write in colloquial language and to polish her own classical prose style, and her works The Last Day of the Year (1894) and the masterpiece Takekurabe (1895).

National Diet Library, Japan, 'HIGUCHI Ichiyo', Portraits of Modern Japanese Historical Figures (English biographical note, read in full, about 150 words). Library biography: entered the Haginoya poetry academy in 1886, began writing stories under a mentor in 1891, the 1892 breakthrough 'Umoregi' and contacts with the Bungakkai literary circle, a household-goods shop run to earn a living, the novels The Last Day of the Year (1894), Muddy Bay (1895) and Growing Up (1895), and her diaries. The page also hosts the library's portraits of her.

Yamamoto Kinji, 'Higuchi Ichiyō: A Pioneer of Modern Japanese Literature', Nippon.com (Shapers of Japanese History series, 2 May 2022; read in full, about 2,300 words). Detailed popular biography from the Nippon Communications Foundation: self-directed waka study after leaving school, the Haginoya academy, her 1892 debut under a mentor, early stories described as conventional love tragedies that won no particular attention, a period of running a shop beside the Yoshiwara quarter that became the setting of Takekurabe, library visits, the burst of work in 'the miraculous 14 months', and Mori Ogai's praise of Takekurabe. Family, health and romantic passages were read but are not used.

Art & Culture Foundation of Taito, 'Ichiyo Memorial Museum' (facility page, read in full, about 450 words). Museum account of her years running a small general store in Ryusenji, the origin of Takekurabe in that neighbourhood, Mori Ogai's praise of the work, and the museum's holdings of her manuscripts, poem cards, letters and desk. Institutional and commemorative in tone; its statement that she never gave up writing is the museum's own phrasing.

Matthew Hernon, 'Spotlight: Ichiyo Higuchi - The Face of the 5,000 Yen Note', Tokyo Weekender (23 November 2022; read in full, about 1,100 words). English-language culture-magazine profile: top marks at school and at the poetry academy, the shop beside the Yoshiwara quarter and its role as inspiration for Takekurabe, her continued writing while busy at the shop, her hesitancy to release stories she was not satisfied with, translations and film adaptations, and her appearance on the banknote. Some totals (21 short stories) differ from Nippon.com (24) and were not used. Passages on her health and private life were not used.

Elaine Gerbert, review of Timothy J. Van Compernolle, 'The Uses of Memory: The Critique of Modernity in the Fiction of Higuchi Ichiyo' (Harvard University Asia Center, 2006), Monumenta Nipponica 62(3), 2007 (open portion read at Project MUSE, about 700 words). Scholarly journal review summarising the book's argument that she reworked traditional literary themes and tropes to critique modernity and opened 'an alternative path' for modern Japanese literature, and noting two earlier critical traditions (one on her premodern style, one on modern and feminist themes). It reports the book's thesis, so it is secondary evidence of scholarly opinion rather than an independent test of her originality.
Wikipedia, 'Higuchi Ichiyō' (consulted for orientation only; never counted as a source and not used as support for any row).

persistence.rationale: [src_higuchi_nippon, src_higuchi_tw, src_higuchi_museum, src_higuchi_ndl | 1891-1896 | popular biography + culture magazine + museum + library] Nippon.com says that after the family opened a shop beside the Yoshiwara quarter she did not give up fiction, left her sister minding the store when she went to the library, and kept writing and was asked for contributions by people at the Bungakukai magazine; Tokyo Weekender says that despite being busy at the shop she did not give up writing; the museum says she never gave up being a novelist; the library records the 1892 breakthrough, the shop and the 1894-95 novels. Continued writing alongside other work is documented; the descriptions of her resolve come from commemorative or popular accounts, and no hardship or personal loss is used as a basis.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_higuchi_nippon, src_higuchi_tw, src_higuchi_brit, src_higuchi_ndl | 1884-1895 | popular biography + culture magazine + reference + library] Nippon.com says that after leaving school she took correspondence courses in waka and kept learning alone at her desk, then stood out for her waka at the Haginoya academy; Tokyo Weekender says she was regularly top of the class there and was hesitant to release stories she was not satisfied with; Britannica says she studied classical literature at a poetry school for several years and then polished her own classical prose style; the library records her entry to the academy in 1886. Study and craft refinement are documented; the evidence for her level of mastery is praise, with no independent assessment of her scholarship.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_higuchi_brit, src_higuchi_nippon, src_higuchi_mn | 1891-1895 | reference + popular biography + scholarly review] Britannica says she ignored her mentor's chief suggestion to write in colloquial language and instead polished her own distinctive classical prose; Nippon.com says her immersion in the Yoshiwara neighbourhood changed the subjects of her stories after her first mentor had taught her popular fiction; the review of Van Compernolle's book summarises the argument that she took 'an alternative path' by reworking the literary heritage. The stylistic decision rests on one sentence in one reference work and the scholarly reading is a reviewer's summary of a thesis, so the row is modest.

creative_originality.rationale: [src_higuchi_brit, src_higuchi_nippon, src_higuchi_museum, src_higuchi_mn | 1892-1896 | reference + popular biography + museum + scholarly review] Britannica calls her the most important Japanese woman writer of her period and says her works treated the licensed quarters and women of old downtown Tokyo; Nippon.com says her earlier stories were conventional love tragedies that won little attention until she drew on the shop neighbourhood, and that Takekurabe was acclaimed by Mori Ogai and fixed her place in the canon; the museum repeats Ogai's praise; the Monumenta Nipponica review reports a scholarly argument that she reworked traditional tropes to critique modernity. These are retrospective assessments by admirers and a reviewer summarising a book thesis; no sceptical study was read. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): reviewed as the top-risk row; lowered from 70 / 0.56 to 66 / 0.52 because every source is retrospective praise or commemorative, Ogai's praise reaches us only through secondary accounts, and the scholarly source is a reviewer's summary rather than an independent test.

portrait.source: Oval portrait photograph of Higuchi Ichiyo captioned in print 'Higuchi Ichiyo shoei (Meiji 28)', that is a portrait of 1895, as reproduced in the Japanese literature anthology 'Gendai Nihon bungaku zenshu, vol. 9' (Kaizosha, 1931; National Diet Library digital collection pid 2627917, whose record carries the library's public-domain mark) and displayed on the National Diet Library's digital exhibition 'Portraits of Modern Japanese Historical Figures', page for Higuchi Ichiyo. The photographer is not named. Rights review: the exhibition's current 'About This Site' page states that all images used in the exhibition are in the public domain and may be reused, including commercially, with the source cited (the library notes that its terms were unchanged when its website policy was updated in February 2025). The basis is also age: the photograph dates from 1895, the sitter died in 1896, and it was reproduced in a Japanese book of 1931, so any Japanese term had expired long before the 1996 US restoration date and the image is in the public domain in the United States. Caveats: the individual photographer and the first publication of the photograph were not found; the image is a halftone reproduction. Identity rests on the printed caption. Cropped from the library's 448 x 495 pixel exhibition image to the oval portrait to remove the caption, 344 x 450 pixels (never upscaled). A larger exhibition image from a 1959 biography was not used because its source book is not openly viewable.

The unresolved issue (unknown photographer) remains as a recorded caveat and is covered by the age basis. SELF-REPORT SEPARATION: no diary text is quoted as evidence; a diary line about feeling distress at her writing was read in Tokyo Weekender and deliberately not used. EXCLUSIONS (hard rule): her illness and death, her father's death and the family debts as personality evidence, her family relationships, her engagement, her feelings for her mentor and every private or romantic matter are NOT used and no trait is inferred from them.
